{{short description|British businessman}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2019}}
'''Geoffrey Heyworth, 1st Baron Heyworth''' (18 October 1894 – 15 June 1974), was a British businessman and [[public servant]].

At the outbreak of [[World War I]], he was employed as an [[accountant]] in [[Toronto]], Canada. He served as a [[lieutenant]] in [[134th Battalion, CEF]] 1916/1919. He was [[wounded in action]] in France on 14 July, 1918.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://central.bac-lac.gc.ca/.item/?op=pdf&app=CEF&id=B4315-S005|title=Officers' Declaration Paper: Canadian Over-Seas Expeditionary Force.|date=3 October 1916|access-date=25 April 2026}}</ref>

Heyworth was chairman of [[Imperial Chemical Industries]]<ref name="mills">{{cite book|title=Difficult Folk?: A Political History of Social Anthropology |author=David Mills }}</ref> and of [[Unilever]],<ref name="gazette3june1955">{{London Gazette |issue=40497 |date=3 June 1955 |page=3257 }}</ref> a company for which he worked for 48 years until his retirement in 1960.<ref>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2507&dat=19600427&id=_ys1AAAAIBAJ&sjid=2KULAAAAIBAJ&pg=4662,7739053 ''The Glasgow Herald'', 27 April 1960. "Tributes to Lord Heyworth on His Retirement".]</ref> He was also a member of the [[National Coal Board]] and the [[London Passenger Transport Board]].<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=39688 |date=4 November 1952 |page=5823 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=30 May 1946 |title=Personal |url= |journal=Passenger Transport Journal |volume=96 |issue= |pages=344 |doi= |access-date=}}</ref> In 1951, he was appointed to a commission, led by [[Lionel Cohen, Baron Cohen|Sir Lionel Cohen]], set up to look into the issue of taxation on income and profits.<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=39119 |date=9 January 1951 |page=192 }}</ref> Having been [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in 1948,<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=38360 |date=23 July 1948 |page=4197}}</ref> he was raised to the peerage as '''Baron Heyworth''' on 25 July, 1955, of Oxton in the County Palatine of Chester,<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=40549 |date=29 July 1955 |page=4360 }}</ref> in recognition of his "... public services".<ref name="gazette3june1955"/> He was the lead author of ''[[The Heyworth Report]]'' (1965), which led to the establishment of the [[Social Science Research Council]].<ref name="mills"/> He was also [[List of presidents of the Royal Statistical Society|President of the Royal Statistical Society]] from 1949 to 1950.<ref>[http://www.rss.org.uk/site/cms/contentviewarticle.asp?article=486 www.rss.org.uk Past Presidents] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120317044817/http://www.rss.org.uk/site/cms/contentviewarticle.asp?article=486 |date=17 March 2012 }}</ref>

Lord Heyworth died in June 1974, aged 79.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Woodroofe |first=Ernest |author-link=Ernest Woodroofe |title=Obituary: Lord Heyworth of Oxton |url=https://academic.oup.com/jrsssa/article/137/4/643/7104713 |access-date=25 April 2026 |via=[[Oxford Academic]]|date=July 1974|journal=[[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society]]|issue=4|volume=137|pages=643, 644}}</ref> The barony died with him.{{citation needed|date=September 2019}}
